cannot_tell.text: The studies measured their effects three or more years after each reform. The model places that effect inside 2027–2031, the law's first five years. Much of a real law's effect may come after 2031, so the yearly path is the least certain part of these numbers.

rows.text: The suburbs' room for new homes is estimated from existing buildings and not scaled by 0.719.

rows.text: Buses every 15 minutes do not qualify. Fewer homes are near stops, so fewer homes are expected near stops both with and without the law.

rows.text: The Census permit file misses most of Milwaukee's apartments; the main case uses the city's property file instead.

trace.part: Bus and train stops, and how often buses come
trace.text: Stop locations from the federal National Transit Map; frequencies from each agency's own schedule file or, for Madison, its published route descriptions.
2020 census homes in blocks whose centre lies within the distance: 313,564 homes in the main case.
Each place's expected new homes under current law (Census building permits, 2023–2025 average, with Milwaukee's apartments counted from its property records), times its share of homes near stops.

Each scenario's share of the homes near stops comes from a published study of a whole city's net gain in homes after upzoning (Los Angeles, 1,136 US cities, Auckland), divided by the study's coverage where it reports one.

trace.part: That those results carry over to Wisconsin
trace.text: No Wisconsin outcome has tested the sizing. Milwaukee's and Madison's shares of homes near stops (68% and 63%) are close to Los Angeles's 61% coverage.
The little and typical responses follow the build-up measured after the New York rezonings; the strong response follows Auckland's own yearly pattern.

trace.part: Where homes land in Milwaukee and Madison
trace.text: From the two cities' zoning codes, entered rule by rule: the extra floor area the law allows on each piece of land. These two cities get 41% of the typical response.

trace.part: Where homes land in the suburbs
trace.text: Their zoning rules were not entered, so the room for new homes is estimated from existing buildings and scaled by 0.719, the ratio measured in Milwaukee and Madison. The suburbs get 59% of the typical response.
Each place's numbers are split across districts in proportion to where its detached houses are (the same split the ADU screens use), not by homes near stops.
